newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli shares end mixed in roller-coaster trade.
newsitem.headline: Israeli shares end mixed in roller-coaster trade.

text.p: Israeli shares closed mixed on Monday in volatile trading after recovering from early losses in response to the shekel's sharp drop against the dollar, traders said.
The benchmark Mishtanim index of the top 100 shares ended down 0.19 percent, or 0.56 points, to 296.35 on all-share turnover of 229 million shekels against 265 million shekels on Sunday.
The Maof 25 blue chip index closed 0.21 percent higher at 304.69.

"The session opened with heavy supply as investors took profits and the index fell by 1.5 percent. Towards the end of the trading day the market started rising sharply following the decline of the shekel against the dollar," said Yossi Weidelfeld of Eyal Securities.
The representative rate for the dollar was fixed on Monday at 3.4840 shekels against 3.4370 on Friday.

Traders said export-oriented companies are expected to be the main gainers from the shekel's decline. "Exporters shares and Israeli shares that are also traded in New York will become more attractive. The heavy-capitalisation stocks led the market's recovery," Weidelfeld said.

"The rise of the shekel prevented the market from falling today despite the fact that mutual funds sold almost 30 million shekels today as investors started taking profits," said a trader at the First International Bank of Israel.
"The fact that even on a day like this the market did not fall is another indicator of its strength," Weidelfeld added.

The most active shares were Teva Pharmaceutical Industries, which gained 0.75 percent to 22,917 agorot on volume of 18.7 million shekels; Bank Leumi, which fell 0.25 percent at 569 agorot on turnover of 17.1 million shekels; and Bank Hapoalim, which rose 1.0 percent to 772 agorot on volume of 12.6 million shekels.
A spokesman for Ted Arison said on Monday that a group led by Arison Investments will begin negotiations with the Israeli government in the next several days on its bid for Hapoalim.

The spokesman would not confirm or deny a report in the Israeli daily Haaretz that the group would offer between $825 million and $890 million for a third of the shares in Israel's largest bank. At that level, the offer values the bank at no more than $2.67 billion, less than its present market capitalisation of $2.8 billion.
-- Dan Gerstenfeld, Tel Aviv newsroom, 972-3-537-2211 x233
